sourceNotes: Seeded from PHT roleplay performance indicators and hospitality and tourism cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: PHT event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the hospitality and tourism cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Counted only when a trip outside the usual environment lasts at least one night but under twelve months, and the main purpose is not paid work for an employer resident in the place visited — all three tests must hold or the trip is not tourism at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a traveller profile — a consultant on a two-year posting, a student on a nine-month exchange — and ask whether the destination may count the person in its arrivals; only the twelve-month and employment tests settle it.

terms.definition: Crosses into the destination and leaves without an overnight stay, so the trip enters visitor arrivals but produces zero bed-nights — which is why a cruise or border town can post huge arrival counts against almost no lodging demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a port town brags about 400,000 arrivals but its hotels sit at 45% occupancy is solved by separating same-day visitors from overnight ones before recommending any lodging investment.

terms.definition: Bounded by routine rather than distance — places a person reaches frequently and habitually, such as the commute to work or school and regular shopping trips, are inside it, so those journeys are never tourism no matter how many miles or borders they cross.
terms.whyItMatters: Statistics questions ask why a worker crossing a national border daily is excluded from tourism counts while a resident's weekend trip 40 miles away is included; frequency, not mileage, draws that line.

terms.definition: Standardized set of national-accounting tables that sizes tourism by matching visitor demand against each supplying industry's output, because tourism is a demand-side concept and therefore has no industry line of its own in the national accounts.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case asks how a country can claim tourism is 8% of GDP with no 'tourism industry' in its statistics, the answer is the satellite account's demand-to-supply reconciliation, not a survey.

terms.definition: For one product or industry, the share of its total domestic supply that visitors actually buy — internal tourism consumption divided by total supply — so a restaurant sector at 0.22 has 22% of its output attributed to tourism.
terms.whyItMatters: Any exam item that asks how much of a city's restaurant or taxi revenue counts as tourism is answered by applying this ratio, not by counting the businesses that call themselves tourist-facing.

terms.definition: Sums each industry's gross value added multiplied by its tourism ratio, plus net taxes on tourism products, so only the visitor-served slice of every supplier counts — deliberately excluding the supplier-chain and wage-respending effects some lobby figures fold in.
terms.whyItMatters: A judge asking why an association's '10% of GDP' claim differs from the government's 4% is testing whether you know the direct measure stops before indirect and induced contributions.

terms.definition: One person spending one night, so a couple staying three nights in a single room generates six of them against only three room-nights — the unit almost every destination statistic is divided by, and the reason per-unit figures differ wildly depending on which one was used.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing an occupancy report to a destination's visitor-spend-per-night figure goes wrong immediately unless you notice one counts rooms and the other counts people.

terms.definition: Total guest-nights divided by total arrivals, which means a destination raises it only by keeping the same visitors longer — adding arrivals with the same trip pattern leaves it flat while multiplying congestion and arrival-processing cost.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay where a bureau wants higher yield without more crowding, this is the metric you move, and you must show the division to prove new arrivals would not do it.

terms.definition: Expresses visitor pressure as the average number of visitors present on a typical day per 1,000 residents — annual bed-nights divided by 365, divided by resident population, times 1,000 — so a small island can outrank a capital city that hosts far more people.
terms.whyItMatters: Carrying-capacity and resident-sentiment questions require a per-resident measure; raw arrival totals rank destinations by size and hide exactly the pressure the question is about.

terms.definition: Tourist bed places times 100, divided by resident population: below 10 the place is barely a destination, and above 100 there are more tourist beds than residents, the accepted quantitative line for a community whose housing stock now serves visitors first.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify a short-term-rental cap to a town council, the 100 threshold turns 'too touristy' into a defensible number the council can legislate against.

terms.definition: Reads the Lorenz curve of monthly arrivals as a single figure from 0, where every month is identical, to 1, where a year's demand lands in one month — letting a 200,000-visitor town and a 20-million city be compared on concentration alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Peak-month share flatters big destinations; when a case asks which of two resorts has the worse seasonality problem, the concentration figure is the only comparison that survives the size difference.

terms.definition: Site area divided by the space one visitor needs, multiplied by daily turnover — open hours divided by average visit length — giving the absolute ceiling of bodies a site can hold in a day before any ecological or social correction is applied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay capping daily entries to a historic site expects the arithmetic: a 2,000 m2 courtyard at 4 m2 per visitor, open 10 hours with 2-hour visits, is 500 x 5 = 2,500 visitors, then corrected downward.

terms.definition: Segments brands — never individual properties — into luxury, upper upscale, upscale, upper midscale, midscale and economy by the brand's system-wide average room rate, so a flagship and a roadside unit of the same flag are reported in the same tier, and independents are classed separately regardless of price.
terms.whyItMatters: Building a competitive comparison, students wrongly slot a high-rate suburban property into luxury; the segment follows the flag, and a misassigned tier invalidates every benchmark drawn from it.

terms.definition: Awards European stars from a points catalogue with mandatory minimums per class — roughly 90 points for one star, 170 for two, 250 for three, 380 for four and 570 for five — and revalidates every three years, so stars there are earned against a checklist, not assigned by a magazine.
terms.whyItMatters: A guest disputing that a German three-star is 'worse' than an American one is answered by explaining that European stars measure facilities against a points minimum while U.S. ratings measure inspected service.

terms.definition: Scored by anonymous unannounced inspectors against roughly 900 objective standards, weighted about 75% toward service delivery and only 25% toward facilities — which is why a modest property can out-rate a lavish one that fails on staff interaction.
terms.whyItMatters: When an owner proposes a renovation to chase a fifth star, the weighting tells you training and service recovery move the score far more than marble does.

terms.definition: Right to retain a non-paying guest's baggage as security for the bill without going to court first, and after statutory notice to sell it — a possessory remedy that dies the moment the property leaves the hotel's hands, and that in most states cannot reach clothing the guest is wearing.
terms.whyItMatters: A judge asking what a front-office manager may do when a departing guest refuses to settle expects this remedy and its limits, not a threat to call police over a civil debt.

terms.definition: Caps what a hotel owes for a guest's valuables, commonly a few hundred to a thousand dollars, but only if the property actually offers a safe and posts the statute conspicuously where guests will see it — miss the posting and common-law liability as an insurer of guest goods returns in full.
terms.whyItMatters: In a lost-jewelry roleplay the whole answer turns on whether the notice was posted in the guest room and at registration; the cap is not automatic.

terms.definition: Latin test for whether goods are 'within the inn' — once the property accepts custody, as when a bellhop takes luggage before check-in or valet parks a car, strict liability attaches even though the guest has not yet registered or has already checked out.
terms.whyItMatters: Claims for a car emptied in valet parking or bags stolen from the bell stand hinge on custody, not on whether the person was a registered guest at that moment.

terms.definition: Number of consecutive nights — commonly 30 in U.S. jurisdictions — after which an occupant stops being a guest and becomes a tenant, at which point lodging tax normally ceases and removal requires a court eviction instead of a lockout.
terms.whyItMatters: A long-stay resident refusing to leave cannot lawfully be locked out once past the threshold, and the exam tests whether you know the day count changed the legal relationship.

terms.definition: Sets required accessible rooms by property size on a fixed table — 1 for a 25-room hotel, 2 up to 50, 4 up to 75, 5 up to 100 — with roll-in shower rooms required only once a property passes 50 rooms, and the counts dispersed across room types and rates.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a planned 60-room build complies, you need the table and the dispersion rule; a designer who puts all accessible rooms in the cheapest category still fails.

terms.definition: Requires a carrier to give passengers a chance to leave the aircraft after three hours on a domestic flight and four on an international one, with food and water by the two-hour mark and working lavatories throughout, enforced by per-passenger civil penalties.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling stranded arrivals in a group-travel roleplay, you must know the deplaning clock and the two-hour service duty before advising a client what the airline owes.

terms.definition: Caps an international carrier's exposure for lost, damaged or delayed bags at roughly 1,288 special drawing rights per passenger, and the claim is barred unless filed in writing within 7 days of damage or 21 days of delayed delivery — a currency-indexed ceiling, not a dollar one.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose bag is destroyed abroad recovers nothing after the written-notice window closes, so the counselor's first act is calendar arithmetic, not a claim form.

terms.definition: Traces resident attitudes toward visitors through four deteriorating stages — euphoria, apathy, annoyance and antagonism — as tourism volume rises relative to community tolerance.
terms.whyItMatters: Community-relations roleplays about local backlash expect you to name the stage a town has reached before proposing a mitigation.

terms.definition: Maps a destination's evolution through exploration, involvement, development, consolidation and stagnation, after which it either rejuvenates or declines — the branch point, not the sequence, is what management decisions turn on.
terms.whyItMatters: A destination case describing flat visitor numbers and aging infrastructure is asking you to identify stagnation and argue for a rejuvenation strategy.

terms.definition: Room rate bundling breakfast plus one other meal, normally dinner — two meals, against three under the American Plan, a continental breakfast only under the Continental Plan, and none at all under the European Plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Quoting a resort package requires naming the plan precisely; a guest who expected lunch included under a two-meal plan produces exactly the complaint a service-recovery roleplay is built on.

terms.definition: Replaces a single visitor-number ceiling with monitored indicators and an agreed standard for each, so management acts when an indicator crosses its standard rather than when a headcount is hit — conceding that any use causes change and only the amount is negotiable.
terms.whyItMatters: When a site's carrying-capacity number is politically impossible to enforce, this framework is the alternative you propose, and you must state the indicators you would monitor.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: An orderly, methodical approach to tasks and decisions that follows a logical structure.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges favor structured reasoning over a scattered approach.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: Scott's grid crossing caring personally with challenging directly: high on both is candor, caring without challenging is ruinous empathy that withholds the correction that would have helped, challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression, and neither is manipulative insincerity. The named failure most managers actually commit is the first, not harshness.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a well-liked employee is quietly underperforming is scored on delivering the specific correction, since softening it to protect the relationship is the graded mistake.

terms.definition: Makes an employer vicariously liable for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment even though the employer itself did nothing careless. A minor deviation from the route or task — a detour — stays inside that scope, while a substantial personal errand — a frolic — falls outside it, and a genuine independent contractor generally does not trigger the doctrine at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Agency roleplays about a delivery driver's crash ask whether the company pays, and the frolic-versus-detour line decides it.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Standard measure of non-degree instruction in which one unit equals 10 contact hours of participation in an accredited program, so a two-day 16-hour seminar earns 1.6 units. A college credit hour is a different currency entirely — roughly 15 contact hours across a semester — and licensing boards rarely convert one into the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked on the exam to price a training plan against a 40-hour renewal requirement, a competitor has to convert seminar hours into units before the budget makes sense.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: Gable's strongest of four ways to answer someone's good news, formed by crossing active with passive and constructive with destructive: responding actively and constructively means asking questions that let the person relive the event, while passive-constructive is a flat nice job, active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive changes the subject. Only the first strengthens the relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays on recognizing a team member's contribution are scored on a specific, curious response in the moment rather than a generic congratulation or a deferred award.

terms.definition: The exposure of a bondholder to rate changes: when market rates rise, existing bonds paying the older lower rate fall in price, and longer maturities fall further.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why an investment roleplay calls long-term bonds risky for a client who may need the money early, despite the bonds being fully repaid at maturity.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining relationships with professionals to exchange knowledge and opportunity.
terms.whyItMatters: Networking is essential for discovering and advancing career opportunities.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: Letting one strong impression, often a single outstanding trait, lift every unrelated rating for the same person; its inverse, the horns effect, drags them all down from one bad impression. In an appraisal it shows up as suspiciously uniform scores across dimensions that ought to vary, and the standard counter is rating every employee on one dimension at a time before moving to the next.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows an evaluation form with identical scores in every category is testing this, and an HR roleplay on fixing a review process is scored on the dimension-by-dimension fix.

terms.definition: The wages, salaries, bonuses, and other financial rewards given for work.
terms.whyItMatters: Fair, competitive pay attracts talent, motivates performance, and aids retention.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: Licensing threshold most states impose on CPA candidates: 150 semester hours of college credit — 30 beyond the 120 a bachelor's degree typically carries — plus all four sections of the Uniform CPA Exam and a year of supervised experience. Several states now allow a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience as an alternate route to the same license.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting-designations roleplay asks what a college junior must still complete before licensure; the answer is a credit count and an exam, not a job offer.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: Deci and Ryan's account of motivation as three psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — plus a continuum running from purely external regulation through introjected and identified regulation to fully internalized motivation. Motivation is therefore a location on that continuum rather than an amount, and only the internalized end keeps working once the supervisor stops watching.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why a bonus program stopped producing results, or a roleplay on motivating a team without extra budget, is scored on giving choice, competence feedback and belonging instead of raising the payout.

terms.definition: An instruction that suspends the retention schedule and freezes every document touching anticipated or filed litigation, overriding routine destruction until counsel lifts it; skipping it exposes the company to spoliation sanctions under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) even when the deletion was only the ordinary schedule running as designed.
terms.whyItMatters: In a legal-issues roleplay where a customer has threatened suit, the first correct action is stopping automatic email deletion — not gathering documents after the subpoena arrives.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: Damping an emotion after it has already arrived by hiding its outward signs, rather than changing the interpretation that produced it. Because it is applied late, it leaves the physiological arousal fully intact, raises blood pressure in the person watching as well, and measurably impairs memory for what was said during the episode -- the opposite profile from cognitive reappraisal, which is applied early and carries none of those costs.
terms.whyItMatters: When a Human Resources Management Series judge asks how you would hold composure while an employee vents about a denied raise, an answer built on hiding what you felt names the strategy research links to worse recall of the conversation; the scoring answer reinterprets the outburst before it peaks.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Investment credential awarded after passing three sequential exams, each historically about six hours, and documenting 4,000 hours of qualified work experience earned over a minimum of 36 months. It certifies analytical competence only: unlike a CPA license it grants no legal authority to audit financial statements or sign a tax return.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-finance roleplay explaining designations to an intern, the tested contrast is that this one signals analysis while the CPA license signals attest authority.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: Book inventory value minus counted physical value, divided by book value (or by net sales), expressed as a percentage — it isolates loss to theft, damage, spoilage and paperwork error, and never includes units legitimately sold.
terms.whyItMatters: Loss-prevention items give a recorded value and a counted value and ask for the percentage lost; the retail benchmark of roughly one to two percent of sales is what a judge compares your figure against.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Two-part credential in financial planning, analysis and strategic decision support, requiring a bachelor's degree, two years of management-accounting experience, and 30 continuing hours a year of which 2 must be ethics. It is built for internal decision support, whereas the CPA license exists for the external attest work a CMA holder may not sign.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay asking which credential fits a cost-analyst career path needs this internal-versus-external split stated with its hour requirement.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: Two or more firms creating a jointly owned legal entity with its own capital, governance, and shared profits for a defined purpose; a strategic alliance is a contractual cooperation with no new entity and no equity exchanged, so it is faster to form and far easier to unwind.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe two companies co-building a plant under a new company name and expect the entity distinction, with 'alliance' planted as the near-miss.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: Plan language reversing commission already paid when the customer cancels or fails to pay inside a stated chargeback window — often 90 days for non-payment or the first 12 months of a subscription. Once that window closes the money is the rep's to keep, so the length of the window, not the cancellation itself, decides whether the company recovers anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics-and-compensation items ask what happens when a rep sells to a customer who churns in month two, and the answer depends on the window; a roleplay on writing a commission plan is graded on naming one.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: How far sales can fall before the firm hits break-even: (actual or budgeted sales - break-even sales) / actual sales. A 12% figure means a 13% sales decline puts the operation into a loss, which is why a lender reads it next to the break-even volume rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-plan defense questions ask how risky a sales forecast is, and this ratio answers that in one number a judge can check.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Freedom from any relationship that would let a firm review its own work: Sarbanes-Oxley bars nine categories of non-audit service for an audit client, forces the lead partner off the engagement after five years, and imposes a one-year cooling-off period before an auditor may join that client as CFO or controller. Objectivity is a mindset; this is the enforceable rule set.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay in which the audit firm is offered the client's bookkeeping work is decided by these prohibitions, not by whether the team feels unbiased.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: Member-governed body that publishes a code of ethics, administers credentialing exams and sets practice standards for a field — the AICPA for accountants, SHRM for HR professionals. A labor union may cover overlapping workers but bargains collectively over wages and conditions; an association negotiates nothing and its only sanction is revoking the credential.
terms.whyItMatters: The accounting roleplay that asks what a professional organization does for a member is scored on services and enforcement, and confusing it with a union loses the item.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Duty a broker-dealer owes to recommend products that fit a customer's stated objectives, raised in 2020 to a best-interest obligation requiring conflicts to be disclosed. It still stops short of the fiduciary standard a registered investment adviser owes under the Advisers Act of 1940, where the client's interest comes first continuously, not only at the moment of a recommendation.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-advising roleplay about recommending a higher-commission fund turns on which of the two duties the professional is actually held to.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Binds a principal to a deal because the principal's own words or conduct led a third party to believe reasonably that the agent was authorized, even though no actual authority — express or implied — was ever granted. The manifestation must trace back to the principal, not to the agent's own claims, which is why an agent who simply asserts power creates none.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a terminated sales rep still carries company cards and signs an order tests this against actual authority.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Statement of the principles a profession owes the public, enforced by a licensing or membership board that can suspend or revoke the credential itself. A code of conduct is narrower and employer-issued: it lists prohibited acts and is enforced through progressive discipline up to termination, which ends the job but leaves the right to practice intact.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where an employee follows company policy yet violates a professional standard requires naming which body can act and what each can take away.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: A contract paying a fixed stream of income for a set term or for life, bought with a lump sum — insurance against outliving savings rather than an investment for growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement roleplays raise it for a client who fears running out of money, and its trade-off is giving up access to the principal.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: Statutory shield for an employee who reports suspected fraud: Sarbanes-Oxley gives a retaliation complaint 180 days to reach OSHA, while Dodd-Frank pays an SEC tipster 10% to 30% of sanctions when the recovery exceeds $1 million. Reporting internally first preserves the retaliation claim but is not a precondition of the SEC award.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-ethics roleplay about a coworker's falsified expense reports, the graded answer names the channel and the filing window, not just 'tell someone'.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: (Range maximum minus range minimum) divided by the minimum, times 100 — a grade running $40,000 to $60,000 has a 50% spread. Spreads widen as jobs get bigger: roughly 30 to 40% for clerical grades, 40 to 50% for professionals and 50% or more for executives, because senior jobs give a long-tenured performer more room to grow in pay without a promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Structuring a pay grade in a compensation roleplay requires setting the minimum and maximum from the midpoint and the intended spread, a calculation judges look for explicitly.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: Stretch of the calendar when insiders may not trade their own company's stock, typically closing two to four weeks before quarter-end and reopening one to two full trading days after earnings are released. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is the only clean way around it: trades are pre-scheduled and, under the 2023 amendments, cannot begin for at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay in which an employee wants to sell vested shares the week before an earnings release is answered by the window, not by intent.

terms.definition: Petty and Cacioppo's two-route account of persuasion. An audience with both the motivation and the ability to think takes the central route, where argument quality decides and the resulting attitude is durable and resists counter-argument. An audience missing either one takes the peripheral route, where source attractiveness, the sheer length of the list and mood decide, and the attitude fades quickly. Adding more evidence for a distracted, uninvolved audience therefore changes nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A persuasive-message item that asks why a detailed cost-savings memo convinced the CFO but not the frontline staff is asking which route each audience was on.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: A systematic review of external conditions, competitor activity, and market trends.
terms.whyItMatters: Scanning the environment lets competitors spot opportunities and threats before deciding.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: Flat daily travel allowance that substitutes for itemized receipts — the federal standard for the continental U.S. runs near $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidentals, with the first and last travel days paid at 75% of the meal portion. Anything paid above the published rate becomes taxable wages to the traveler.
terms.whyItMatters: A hospitality or sales roleplay budgeting a three-day trip needs the arithmetic: two full days at the meal rate plus two partial days at three quarters of it.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: Dollar ceiling below which accepting a business courtesy is not treated as influence — federal ethics rules cap it at $20 per occasion and $50 per source per year, and many corporate policies copy those figures. Above the line the item must be refused, returned, or reported, and splitting one gift across two occasions is itself the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A purchasing roleplay where a vendor sends playoff tickets is scored on whether the competitor applies the stated dollar limit and the reporting step.

terms.definition: A classical four-question procedure for locating the exact point at which two sides disagree: conjecture (did it happen?), definition (what should it be called?), quality (how serious is it?) and policy (what should be done about it?). Arguing at the wrong level is the standard failure - answering 'what should we do' while the other side is still disputing whether anything happened produces two speeches that never touch.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge in a conflict roleplay disputes your facts and you answer with a solution, you lose points for never meeting the objection; this names the level you skipped.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: Coordination among suppliers, makers, and distributors to optimize flow and cut cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Collaboration reduces delays and strengthens competitive advantage.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: Post-employment restriction barring a departing worker from joining a competitor for a stated period and geography, commonly 6 to 12 months. Enforceability is a state question — California voids them outright and several states exempt hourly workers below a wage threshold — and a court will usually narrow an unreasonable radius rather than rewrite the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising an employee who has an offer from a rival turns on this clause's scope and on whether the state will enforce it at all.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: Ten observed roles grouped in three sets — interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson), and decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator) — describing what managers actually do in fragmented bursts rather than the tidy plan-organize-lead-control cycle.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items quote a manager's activity and ask which role category it belongs to, so the three groupings must be recalled by name.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: Reimbursement arrangement that keeps expense payments out of taxable wages, valid only when the expense has a business connection, is substantiated with receipts within 60 days, and any excess advance is returned within 120 days. Miss any one of the three and the arrangement is non-accountable, so every reimbursed dollar is added to the W-2 and taxed as pay.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on a sales rep who never turns in travel receipts is really asking why the reimbursement showed up as taxable income.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Withholding certificate an employee files so the employer deducts the right federal income tax; the 2020 redesign dropped allowances for a five-step worksheet stated in dollars, including $2,000 per qualifying child. It is not Form I-9, which proves work authorization within three business days of hire, nor Form W-9, which an independent contractor files instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A first-day onboarding roleplay is scored on knowing which of the three forms does what, since a competitor who names the wrong one has the new hire unpaid or unauthorized.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged.
