The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: Under the UCC a seller sheds merchantability only with conspicuous language that actually uses the word merchantability, or with an as-is / with-all-faults notice, and sheds fitness for a particular purpose only in writing. An express promise once made cannot be disclaimed at all — fine print cannot cancel what the salesperson said out loud.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a spoken performance promise with an as-is sticker and ask which survives; a product-selling roleplay is scored on not making a claim the contract cannot later walk back.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: Narrower post-employment restriction that lets a departing worker take any job but forbids contacting the former employer's customers or recruiting its staff, usually for 12 to 24 months. Because it limits whom you may approach rather than where you may work, courts enforce it in states that will not enforce a non-compete at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay about a rep who leaves and calls his old book of business is decided by this clause, not by the broader competition ban.

terms.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical syllogism, in which one premise is deliberately left unspoken because the audience already believes it and will supply it themselves. 'We should sponsor the tournament - our customers are all high school families' hides the premise that reaching high school families is worth what the sponsorship costs. The unstated premise is where the argument is strongest with a friendly audience and weakest with a hostile one, because attacking what was never said aloud is easier than attacking what was.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that ask what assumption a memo's recommendation rests on are asking you to recover exactly this missing premise.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Continuing to fund a failing course of action in order to justify having chosen it. The dividing line from the sunk-cost fallacy is who is deciding: sunk cost is the reasoning error of counting unrecoverable spend at all, and anyone can make it, while escalation is the behavioral pattern driven by personal responsibility -- managers who personally picked the losing project invest substantially more in it than managers who inherited the same project.
terms.whyItMatters: The structural fix a judge is listening for in a case about a doomed store opening is handing the continue-or-kill call to someone who did not make the original decision; recommending only 'ignore what we already spent' answers the smaller half of the problem.

terms.definition: Setting price by the value a product delivers rather than its cost.
terms.whyItMatters: It aligns price with customer benefit and market demand.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: State or city rule requiring an employer to publish a good-faith salary range inside the job posting itself, as Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act and New York City's Local Law 32 do. It attacks the gap at the offer stage, whereas the Equal Pay Act of 1963 works after the fact by requiring equal pay for substantially equal work.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay preparing a competitor to negotiate an offer changes completely when the posted range is public, because the anchor is set before the conversation.

terms.definition: In speech act theory (Austin and Searle), the action a speaker performs in saying something - promising, ordering, warning, refusing - as distinct from the locutionary act, which is the literal words and their sense, and the perlocutionary act, which is the effect actually produced in the hearer. 'It is cold in here' is locutionally a remark about temperature, illocutionarily a request, and perlocutionarily successful only if somebody closes the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A service roleplay in which the customer says 'I have been waiting a while' is scored on whether you answer the request rather than the sentence.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: Motivational push-back triggered by a perceived restriction on a freedom, which makes the restricted option more attractive rather than less -- the boomerang result seen when warning labels raise interest and mandates raise resistance. It is distinguishable from ordinary disagreement because the target's preference shifts even when they had no prior stake in the option, so the intensity is about the constraint, not the content.
terms.whyItMatters: Leading-change roleplays hinge on this: announcing a mandatory new system produces opposition from people who never used the old one, and the scoring move is to restore a real choice -- rollout timing, pilot team, tool configuration -- rather than to re-explain the rationale.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: Employment clause transferring to the employer any invention conceived during the job, reaching further than copyright's work-made-for-hire rule because it also captures patents. Statutes such as California Labor Code section 2870 carve out inventions developed entirely on the worker's own time, without company equipment or trade secrets, and unrelated to the employer's business.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay about a side project built after hours is scored on whether the competitor can state the carve-out's three conditions.

terms.definition: A sentence that does not describe an act but carries it out, so it cannot be true or false - only successful or void: 'I accept your offer,' 'I resign,' 'I hereby order 500 units.' Austin's felicity conditions are what make it stick - the right person, the right circumstances, the right form - which is why a casually typed 'agreed' from an authorized employee can create a binding acceptance while a long email full of enthusiasm creates nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask how a staff member bound the company in a chat message turn on this distinction between describing and doing.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Ownership raises valuation: in the classic mug experiments sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers would pay for the identical item, minutes after the mugs were handed out at random. Ordinary supply and demand predicts no such gap, and loss aversion supplies the mechanism -- giving up what you hold is coded as a loss rather than as forgone gain, which is also why a free trial and a trade-in allowance both move the price a buyer accepts.
terms.whyItMatters: In a negotiation roleplay, letting the other side describe the arrangement as theirs before you ask them to change it costs you money; the tested application is sequencing the concession before the sense of ownership forms.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: Paid notice period during which a resigning employee stays on payroll but is kept away from the office, from clients and from starting at a competitor, commonly one to six months. It is enforceable in places that void a bare non-compete precisely because the employer keeps paying — the restraint is bought rather than merely imposed.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising a senior manager on a competitor's offer must separate this paid restriction from an unpaid non-compete, because only one keeps income flowing.

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Overestimating how visible one's internal state is to other people. Speakers certain their nervousness was obvious are rated no more nervous than calm speakers by the audience, and people telling a lie believe they are being read far more than they are. The error concerns inner states specifically -- nerves, doubt, irritation -- which is what separates it from the parallel mistake about outward appearance and conduct.
terms.whyItMatters: A competitor convinced the judge can see their hands shaking starts apologizing for nerves that were never detected, spending scoring time on damage control; the counter is to keep delivering the presentation as planned because the leak is far smaller than it feels.

terms.definition: The charter filed with the secretary of state that brings a corporation into legal existence, stating its name, registered agent, purpose and the number of authorized shares, and amendable only by shareholder vote plus another state filing. Bylaws are the separate internal rulebook — meetings, officers, quorum, notice — adopted by the board, never filed publicly, and changed without any state involvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A venture roleplay asks which document has to change before more shares can be issued to a new investor.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: Department of Labor-registered training program pairing paid on-the-job hours — about 2,000 a year under a journey-worker mentor — with at least 144 hours of related classroom instruction and scheduled wage increases as each skill is certified. An internship carries no registered hour floor, no mentor requirement and no guaranteed wage progression.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to gain real work experience is scored on naming the structured, paid, credentialed route rather than only the summer internship.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: The moral dimension of a decision dropping out of the frame so it gets processed as a budget, legal or scheduling problem instead. The failure is not a person choosing wrong but a person never seeing a choice, which is why euphemism -- 'aggressive accounting', 'creative sourcing' -- is a diagnostic symptom rather than a cosmetic one. It also explains the prediction gap: in one study most participants said they would refuse or confront an improper interview question, and essentially none did when it happened.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making cases are built on decisions already reframed as operational, and the scoring move is to restore the moral question out loud before analyzing the numbers; competitors who answer only the financial framing lose the ethics indicator entirely.

terms.definition: A basket of securities that trades on an exchange throughout the day like a single stock, unlike a mutual fund, which prices once after the market closes.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending one over a mutual fund in an investing roleplay rests on intraday pricing and typically lower costs, not on different holdings.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: Employment term routing disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court, waiving a jury and usually class treatment; the Federal Arbitration Act makes it binding and the award is nearly unappealable on the merits. The 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration Act carves out sexual assault and harassment claims, which an employee may still take to court.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay walking a new hire through an offer packet has to flag what this clause gives up, since signing happens on day one and matters years later.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Overestimating how much observers notice and later recall one's appearance and actions. Wearers of an embarrassing shirt guessed about half the room could identify it; roughly a quarter could. Unlike the illusion of transparency, the misjudgment is about what is visible on the outside -- a stumble, a stain, an awkward entrance -- rather than about the feelings underneath, and the two are tested as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: Fumbling the first line of a roleplay opener feels catastrophic and costs almost nothing on a judge's rubric; competitors who know the size of the gap recover in one sentence instead of carrying the mistake through the remaining nine minutes.

terms.definition: Pay left above the maximum of an employee's grade after a job is re-evaluated downward or a range is lowered — the salary is frozen or paid out as a lump sum instead of a base increase until the range catches up. Its opposite, a green-circled rate, sits below the grade minimum and is corrected by moving the employee up to at least the minimum, usually on a set schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: In a restructuring roleplay you must say what happens to a person whose job was downgraded; freezing base pay rather than cutting it is the answer judges expect.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: Four-quadrant triage that sorts a task list on two separate axes, urgency and importance: important and urgent is handled now, important and not urgent is scheduled and is where career-building work lives, urgent and not important is delegated, and neither is dropped. The insight is that a loud task can rank last.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay handed a full inbox and one afternoon is scored on the quadrant each item lands in and the action that quadrant dictates.

terms.definition: A member's assertion that the rules are being broken at this moment - a motion made out of order, debate wandering off the pending question, a vote miscounted. It may interrupt a speaker, requires no second, is not debatable, and is settled by the chair's ruling rather than a vote, though any two members may appeal that ruling to the assembly. It must be timely: raised after the offending action is complete, it is normally too late.
terms.whyItMatters: Chapter meetings and management roleplays run on a written agenda test whether you know which objections may interrupt a speaker and which must wait for the floor.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: The proposed tendency to explain one's own behavior by circumstances and another's by disposition. It cannot be treated as a restatement of the fundamental attribution error, and the reason is empirical: a meta-analysis of 173 studies found the overall asymmetry close to zero, surfacing mainly for negative or unexpected events. The honest form of the claim is therefore conditional -- the split appears when something went wrong.
terms.whyItMatters: Bias-recognition items on the Business Administration Core exam use the unqualified version as a distractor, and a roleplay about a missed deadline is scored on asking what got in the way before assigning a trait, because that is exactly the case where the asymmetry does show up.

terms.definition: Swapping direct identifiers for tokens while keeping the re-identification key stored separately, which leaves the file still legally personal data under GDPR Article 4(5) and still inside the regulation's reach; true anonymization destroys that key irreversibly, and only then does the data fall out of scope entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-in-data-mining item asks whether replacing customer names with ID numbers lets a firm share the file freely, and the graded answer is that it does not while the key survives.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Sworn statement the CEO and CFO sign with every quarterly and annual report, affirming that it is accurate and that they evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls as of the period's end. Section 906 supplies the teeth: a knowing false certification carries fines up to $5 million and imprisonment up to 20 years.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay about pressure to delay recognizing an expense is answered by naming who personally signs for the numbers and what the penalty is.

terms.definition: Tufte's format for comparison: a grid of miniature charts sharing identical axes, identical scales and identical design, with exactly one variable changing from panel to panel - one region, one month or one product each. Holding the scale constant across every panel is the whole specification, and letting each panel auto-scale to its own data is the most common way the format is faked, because it destroys the comparison it exists to make.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-visualization task that hands you five years of sales across eight stores is scored on choosing this over one line chart with eight tangled series.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Having just done or displayed something creditable makes the next questionable act easier, because the earlier one buys credit against the self-image. It runs opposite to the intuition that good behavior predicts more good behavior: participants who first endorsed a minority candidate afterward favored a white applicant more readily than participants given no chance to establish credentials, so the good act enabled the biased one.
terms.whyItMatters: In an ethics case where a firm cites its diversity award or its donation record while defending a questionable decision, naming the licensing pattern turns a weak 'that is irrelevant' into the analysis a judge scores; it also warns against recommending a visible ethics gesture as the whole remedy.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Allocation of professional growth into three ratios: 70% from challenging on-the-job assignments, 20% from developmental relationships such as coaching and feedback, and only 10% from formal courses. It reframes a development plan away from a training catalog and toward the stretch assignment that produces most of the learning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay building a development plan for a high-potential employee loses points if the whole plan is a list of seminars.

terms.definition: The highest-ranking class of motion in Robert's Rules - adjourn, recess, raise a question of privilege, call for the orders of the day - urgent enough that it may be made while other business is pending and outranks every subsidiary motion. Because it does not relate to the pending question it is undebatable in most forms, and its rank is exactly why a motion to adjourn can be made while an amendment is on the floor but an amendment cannot be made while adjournment is.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask which motion may be made while another is still pending are testing the precedence ladder, and this class is its top rung.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: Blaming an out-group's failures on what its members are like while writing off its successes as luck, special help or an exception -- and reversing both judgments for one's own group. The individual-level attribution error concerns one person; this is its group-level extension, and it is the specific mechanism by which a stereotype survives meeting a counterexample, since the counterexample gets filed away rather than counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on overcoming stereotypes reward naming the filing-as-exception move, and a Human Resources roleplay about a hiring panel that keeps calling qualified candidates from one school 'unusual for their program' is describing this error rather than open prejudice.

terms.definition: A card, bin or electronic signal that authorizes replenishment only after downstream consumption, making it a PULL system — the opposite of material requirements planning, which PUSHES output on a forecast whether or not the next station has consumed the last batch.
terms.whyItMatters: Production questions test the pull-versus-push distinction directly: the signal-driven system builds only what was used, so it is the answer when the scenario complains of piled-up work in process.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: Worker excluded from federal overtime because the job clears both a salary-basis test and a duties test — at least $684 a week, which annualizes to $35,568, plus genuine executive, administrative or professional duties. A non-exempt worker, salaried or not, earns 1.5 times the regular rate beyond 40 hours in a week, and a job title alone never settles the classification.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on worker rights that gives an assistant manager a $700 weekly salary and 50 hours is testing both prongs of this test at once.

terms.definition: A written instruction, issued the moment a company reasonably anticipates a dispute, that suspends every routine deletion schedule and directs named custodians to preserve emails, chat threads, drafts and text messages on the subject. The duty attaches before any complaint is filed, and letting an auto-delete rule keep running past that point is what converts ordinary records management into spoliation, exposing the company to an adverse-inference instruction at trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask what an employee must do with a group chat once a customer threatens to sue are testing this duty and, above all, its trigger point.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Overestimating both the intensity and the duration of a future emotional reaction; the duration half alone is the durability bias, and the two named causes are focalism -- attending only to the focal event and not to everything else that will fill the day -- and immune neglect, discounting how quickly one rationalizes an outcome. Lottery winners and people newly paralyzed converge far closer than either group predicts.
terms.whyItMatters: A risk-of-personal-decisions item asking whether a competitor should take a demanding promotion is testing this: the answer that survives is one that weighs the ordinary days after the change, not the peak of the reaction to it.

terms.definition: Separations during a period divided by average headcount for that period, times 100 — 18 departures against an average of 120 staff gives 15% — and the voluntary portion is tracked separately because it, not the involuntary portion, signals a retention problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Management roleplays open with a turnover figure and expect you to compute or interpret it and split voluntary from involuntary before recommending a fix.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: Inventory of the behaviors a role requires, each rated on a defined proficiency scale — commonly five levels from awareness to expert — with written behavioral anchors describing what each level looks like in practice. A job description lists duties and reporting lines; this states how well, which is what makes it scoreable.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asked to justify why one of two equally experienced candidates is ready for the role needs a scored scale, not an impression.

terms.definition: The measured luminance relationship between text and the background behind it under the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, expressed from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text - 18 point, or 14 point bold - plus 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics; level AAA raises body text to 7:1. Light grey captions and a pale brand colour on a white slide are the two failures that show up most.
terms.whyItMatters: A written event or presentation judged on accessibility is scored on naming the threshold your deck actually meets, not on asserting that the colours look readable.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Warning an employer must send before rejecting an applicant because of a background-check report, enclosing a copy of the report and a summary of rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, then waiting a reasonable interval — five business days is the common practice — so the applicant can dispute an error before the final adverse-action notice issues.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay where a screening report shows a charge that belongs to someone else is scored on this two-notice sequence and the gap between them.

terms.definition: Giving full attention, checking understanding, and responding thoughtfully to a speaker.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect competitors to handle questions and concerns clearly.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: A tiered approval ladder capping how deep each level may cut price before escalating — a rep to 10 percent, a sales manager to 20, a vice president to 30, and anything past that to finance. Margin is protected by who is allowed to sign, not by how well an individual rep negotiates, so a buyer stalling for more has to be moved up the ladder.
terms.whyItMatters: A price-negotiation roleplay where the buyer demands 25 percent off is scored on whether you know you must escalate instead of conceding; pricing items test the ladder as a control on gross margin.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: Promise of company shares delivered on a vesting date and taxed as ordinary income on the full market value at vest — 400 shares vesting at $50 is $20,000 of W-2 wages whether or not a single share is sold. A stock option instead taxes the spread at exercise and is worth nothing while the price sits below the strike, which this grant never is.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two offers in a roleplay is impossible without valuing the equity: the exam wants shares times price times the vesting fraction, plus the tax hit at vest.

terms.definition: A readability score that converts a passage into a U.S. school grade: 0.39 x (total words / total sentences) + 11.8 x (total syllables / total words) - 15.59. Because sentence length is multiplied by 0.39 and syllable count by 11.8, swapping 'utilize' for 'use' moves the score less than splitting one 30-word sentence into two 15-word ones; consumer-facing documents are normally targeted at grade 8 or below.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to rewrite a return policy for shoppers is scored on whether you can name a measurable target and the two levers that hit it, instead of promising to 'make it simpler.'

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: Measures how one product's unit sales respond to a different product's price: %change in quantity of A / %change in price of B. A positive coefficient marks substitutes and a negative one marks complements, whereas own-price elasticity compares a product only against its own price.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing roleplay about a two-item lineup asks what raising the price of one does to the other, and the sign of this coefficient is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: Subtraction run one competency at a time — required proficiency minus current proficiency — with the resulting gaps ranked by size multiplied by how critical the competency is, so a 2-point gap on a critical skill outranks a 3-point gap on a peripheral one. Without the criticality weighting it degenerates into a list of everything someone cannot do.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on assessing your own interests and skills against an employer's expectations is really asking for this weighted subtraction.

terms.definition: A letter layout in which every element - date, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature block - begins flush at the left margin with no indentation, set on one-inch margins with a blank line between parts and no blank-line indents inside paragraphs. Modified block, its near neighbour, moves the date and the closing to start at the horizontal center of the page; semi-block does that and also indents the first line of each paragraph.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting items on the exam give you the same letter three ways and ask which is full block, and written-event submissions lose presentation points for mixing two of the three.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Pay increase tied to a published price index rather than to performance — Social Security's 2.5% raise for 2025 came directly from the CPI-W. Relocation uses the same arithmetic: moving a $60,000 salary to a city with a cost index of 130 against a base of 100 takes $78,000 to hold the same purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a transfer offer to a more expensive city is scored on running the index ratio, not on comparing the two base salaries.

terms.definition: A formal written message with a clear subject, correct grammar, and appropriate tone.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward mastery of email conventions.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: Development instrument that collects ratings from four vantage points — self, manager, peers and direct reports, usually 8 to 12 raters in total — and reports where the self-rating and everyone else's diverge. A performance appraisal is single-source and administrative, feeding pay and promotion, which is exactly why these results are normally kept out of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on using development resources is scored on knowing this tool informs growth, and that folding it into a pay decision makes raters stop being honest.

terms.definition: An arrangement that puts the main idea, request or answer in the very first sentence and places explanation after it - correct for routine requests, good news, and most internal messages, and expected by busy or senior readers. The indirect pattern reverses that into four ordered parts: a neutral buffer, the reasons, the bad news itself stated once, and a goodwill close. Choose by predicted reaction, not by topic: a refusal a reader already expects can still be written directly.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common written-event error is burying a recommendation in paragraph three of a message the reader will happily agree with.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: Respecting and adapting to the values and practices of different cultures.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets a business serve diverse markets and build inclusive teams.

terms.definition: Forbids a director, officer, partner or agent from self-dealing, taking an opportunity that belonged to the enterprise, or competing with the principal, and a challenged transaction is judged on whether it was entirely fair rather than whether it was well reasoned. That standard is the split from the duty of care, where the business judgment rule shields an informed, disinterested, good-faith decision even when it turns out badly.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics roleplays about a manager steering a supply contract to a relative's firm are loyalty problems, not care problems.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.
